paragraphs.simple: Polly lived in one of a long row of houses that were all joined together. One morning she was out in the back garden. A boy climbed up from the garden next door and put his face over the wall. Polly was very surprised. Until now there had never been any children in that house. Only Mr. Ketterley and Miss Ketterley lived there. They were a brother and sister, and they were old and had never married. So Polly looked up, wanting to know more. The strange boy's face was very dirty. It could hardly have been dirtier if he had first put his hands in the earth, then cried, and then dried his face with his hands. In fact, that was very nearly what he had been doing.

paragraphs.context: But what she noticed first was a bright red wooden tray
paragraphs.mainIdea: Polly steps into the strange room. The first thing she notices is a bright red tray with rings on it, in pairs of one yellow and one green.
paragraphs.simple: The room was shaped like an attic, but it was set up as a sitting room. The walls were covered with shelves, and every shelf was full of books. A fire was burning in the fireplace, because it was a very cold, wet summer that year. In front of the fire was a high-backed armchair with its back toward the children. Between the chair and Polly was a big table that filled most of the middle of the room. It was piled with all sorts of things: printed books, books to write in, ink bottles, pens, sealing-wax and a microscope. But Polly first noticed a bright red wooden tray with a number of rings on it. They were in pairs: a yellow one and a green one together, then a little space, and then another yellow one and another green one. They were no bigger than ordinary rings, but no one could help noticing them because they were so bright. They were the most beautiful, shiny little things you can imagine. If Polly had been a very little younger, she would have wanted to put one in her mouth.

paragraphs.context: The high-backed chair in front of the fire moved suddenly

paragraphs.simple: Digory never finished what he was going to say, because at that moment something happened. The high-backed chair in front of the fire suddenly moved, and Uncle Andrew rose up out of it, like a demon in a play coming up out of a trapdoor. It was a frightening sight. They were not in the empty house at all. They were in Digory's own house, in the study they were not allowed to enter. Both children said "O-o-oh" and knew that they had made a terrible mistake. They felt they should have known all along that they had not gone nearly far enough.

By then she disliked ordinary, ignorant people, and so did he. But she and he were interested in the same sort of things. Only a few days before she died, she told him to go to an old desk in her house, open a secret drawer, and bring her a little box that he would find there. The moment he picked up the box, he felt a pricking in his fingers and knew that he held some great secret. She gave it to him. She made him promise that as soon as she was dead, he would burn it, unopened, with certain ceremonies. He did not keep that promise.

paragraphs.simple: Digory stood up. He was not dripping and not out of breath, though you would expect that after being under water. His clothes were perfectly dry. He was standing by the edge of a small pool, not more than ten feet from side to side, in a wood. The trees grew close together and had so many leaves that he could not see the sky. All the light was green light that came through the leaves. It was bright and warm, so there must have been a very strong sun overhead. It was the quietest wood you could imagine. There were no birds, no insects, no animals and no wind. You could almost feel the trees growing. The pool he had just got out of was not the only pool. There were dozens of others, a pool every few yards as far as he could see. You could almost feel the trees drinking the water up with their roots. This wood was very much alive. When Digory tried to describe it afterward, he always said, "It was a rich place: as rich as plumcake."

But after the children had gone a few steps down the room, they came to faces that looked a little different. These were very serious faces. You felt you would have to be very careful how you behaved if you ever met living people who looked like that. Further on, about the middle of the room, they found faces they did not like. These faces looked strong and proud and happy, but they looked cruel. A little further on they looked crueler. Further on again, they were still cruel, but they no longer looked happy. They were even faces without hope, as if the people had done terrible things and had also suffered terrible things. The last figure of all was the most interesting. It was a woman even more richly dressed than the others, and very tall (but every figure in that room was taller than the people of our world). She looked so fierce and proud that it took your breath away. But she was beautiful too. Years afterward, when he was an old man, Digory said he had never in all his life known a woman so beautiful. Then he leaned forward, picked up the hammer and gave the golden bell a light, quick tap. Then he let her go. They fell apart, staring at each other and breathing hard. But even her height was nothing compared with her beauty, her fierceness and her wildness. She looked ten times more alive than most of the people one meets in London. Uncle Andrew was bowing and rubbing his hands and looking extremely frightened. He seemed a very small creature beside the Witch. Yet, as Polly said afterward, there was a sort of likeness between her face and his, something in the look on it. It was the look that all wicked Magicians have, the "Mark" that Jadis had said she could not find in Digory's face. One good thing about seeing the two together was that you would never again be afraid of Uncle Andrew. You would not be afraid of a worm after you had met a rattlesnake, or of a cow after you had met a mad bull.

paragraphs.context: swaying with superb balance as it came at full speed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jadis comes back standing on the roof of a cab, beating the horse. The cab crashes into the lamp-post, and she jumps onto the horse's back.
paragraphs.simple: First came the hansom (a horse cab). There was no one in the driver's seat. Jadis, the Queen of Queens and the Terror of Charn, was standing on the roof, not sitting. She kept her balance very well as it came round the corner at full speed with one wheel in the air. Her teeth showed, her eyes shone like fire, and her long hair streamed out behind her like the tail of a comet. She was beating the horse without mercy. Its nostrils were wide and red, and its sides were spotted with foam. It galloped madly up to the front door, missing the lamp-post by an inch, and then rose up on its back legs. The cab crashed into the lamp-post and broke into several pieces. With a magnificent jump, the Witch had sprung clear just in time and landed on the horse's back. She sat with a leg on each side and leaned forward, whispering things in its ear. They must have been things meant not to make it quiet but to make it wild. In a moment it was on its back legs again, and its cry was like a scream. It was all hoofs and teeth and eyes and tossing mane. Only a splendid rider could have stayed on its back.

paragraphs.context: the blackness overhead, all at once, was blazing with stars
paragraphs.mainIdea: In the dark, many high voices join the first deep voice, and stars appear at the same moment. Digory feels sure that the stars are singing.
paragraphs.simple: Then two wonders happened at the same moment. One was that other voices suddenly joined the first voice, more voices than you could count. They sang with it, but far higher: cold, tingling, silvery voices. The second wonder was that the blackness overhead was suddenly full of bright stars. They did not come out gently one by one, as they do on a summer evening. One moment there was nothing but darkness. The next moment a thousand, thousand points of light jumped out: single stars, groups of stars and planets, brighter and bigger than any in our world. There were no clouds. The new stars and the new voices began at exactly the same time. If you had seen and heard it as Digory did, you would have been quite sure that the stars themselves were singing, and that the first voice, the deep one, had made them appear and made them sing.

paragraphs.context: And as he walked and sang the valley grew green with grass
paragraphs.mainIdea: As Aslan sings a new song, grass and then trees grow across the land. Digory watches the trees grow.
paragraphs.simple: The Lion was walking to and fro in that empty land, singing his new song. It was softer than the song that had called up the stars and the sun. It was a gentle, rippling music. As he walked and sang, the valley turned green with grass. The green spread out from the Lion like a pool. It ran up the sides of the little hills like a wave. In a few minutes it was creeping up the lower slopes of the faraway mountains, making that young world softer every moment. Now the light wind could be heard moving the grass. Soon there were other things besides grass. The higher slopes grew dark with heather. Patches of rougher green appeared in the valley. Digory did not know what they were until one began coming up very close to him. It was a little, spiky thing that put out dozens of arms and covered them with green. It grew about an inch every two seconds. There were dozens of these things all round him now. When they were nearly as tall as he was, he saw what they were. "Trees!" he said.

paragraphs.context: every now and then he would go up to two of them
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan goes among the animals and touches two at a time on the nose. The chosen animals stand in a circle round him, in complete silence.
paragraphs.simple: Digory could no longer hear the Lion, but he could see it. It was so big and bright that he could not take his eyes off it. The other animals did not seem afraid of it. Then Digory heard the sound of hoofs behind him, and the old cab-horse trotted past and joined the other beasts. (The air seemed to have been as good for him as for Uncle Andrew. He no longer looked like the poor old slave he had been in London. He was lifting his feet and holding his head up.) For the first time the Lion was quite silent. He went to and fro among the animals. Every now and then he would go up to two of them, always two at a time, and touch their noses with his own. He touched two beavers among all the beavers, two leopards among all the leopards, and one stag and one deer among all the deer, and he left the rest. Some kinds of animal he passed by altogether. But the pairs he had touched at once left their own kind and followed him. At last he stood still, and all the animals he had touched came and stood in a wide circle around him. The others began to wander away. The chosen animals who stayed were completely silent, with their eyes fixed on the Lion. The cat-like ones gave an occasional twitch of the tail, but otherwise all were still. For the first time that day there was complete silence, except for the noise of running water. Digory's heart beat wildly. He knew that something very serious was going to be done. He had not forgotten his Mother, but he knew that even for her he could not interrupt a thing like this.

paragraphs.context: I give to you forever this land of Narnia
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan gives the land of Narnia and everything in it to the creatures. He tells them not to go back to the ways of the Dumb Beasts, or they will stop being Talking Beasts.
paragraphs.simple: Aslan said in his strong, happy voice, "Creatures, I give you yourselves. I give you this land of Narnia for ever. I give you the woods, the fruits and the rivers. I give you the stars, and I give you myself. The Dumb Beasts that I have not chosen are yours too. Be gentle with them and take care of them. But do not go back to their ways, or you will stop being Talking Beasts. You were taken out of them, and you can go back into them. Do not do so."

paragraphs.context: is seven hours old, a force of evil has already entered it
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan says that a force of evil has already come into his new world, brought by Digory. People of Adam's race must help to put right the harm.
paragraphs.simple: Aslan said, "You see, friends, that before the new, clean world I gave you is seven hours old, a force of evil has already come into it. This Son of Adam woke it and brought it here." All the Beasts, even Strawberry, looked at Digory until he wished the ground would swallow him up. "But do not be sad," Aslan said to the Beasts. "Evil will come of that evil, but it is still a long way off, and I will see to it that the worst falls on me. In the meantime, let us put things in order, so that for many hundred years this will be a happy land in a happy world. Adam's race has done the harm, so Adam's race will help to heal it. Come near, you other two."

paragraphs.context: It is my wish to plant in Narnia a tree
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan says the Witch will come back to Narnia, but not yet. He wants a tree that she will not dare to come near, and Digory must bring the seed for it.
paragraphs.simple: Aslan said, "My son, my son, I know. Grief is great. Only you and I in this land know that yet. Let us be good to one another. But I have to think of hundreds of years in the life of Narnia. The Witch whom you have brought into this world will come back to Narnia again. But it need not be yet. I want to plant in Narnia a tree that she will not dare to come near. That tree will keep Narnia safe from her for many years. So this land will have a long, bright morning before any clouds come over the sun. You must get me the seed from which that tree is to grow."

paragraphs.context: there burst out from the shoulders of Fledge wings that spread
paragraphs.mainIdea: Wings burst out from Fledge's shoulders. He flies up, goes round once, and comes down looking awkward and surprised but extremely pleased.
paragraphs.simple: Then, just as the animals had burst out of the earth, wings burst out from the shoulders of Fledge. They spread and grew, bigger than the wings of eagles, bigger than the wings of swans, and bigger than angels' wings in church windows. The feathers shone chestnut color and copper color. He gave a great sweep with them and jumped into the air. Twenty feet above Aslan and Digory, he snorted, neighed and made little jumps in the air. Then he went round once and dropped to the earth, all four hoofs together. He looked awkward and surprised, but extremely pleased.

paragraphs.context: A terrible thirst and hunger came over him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Digory badly wants to taste the apple and begins to think it might not be wrong. He has already taken one "for others".
paragraphs.simple: It would have been better if Digory had not looked at the apple and smelled it. A terrible thirst and hunger came over him, and a longing to taste that fruit. He quickly put it into his pocket, but there were plenty of others. Could it be wrong to taste one? After all, he thought, the notice on the gate might not have been exactly an order. It might have been only a piece of advice, and who cares about advice? Or even if it was an order, would he be breaking it by eating an apple? He had already done what it said about taking one "for others."

paragraphs.context: There, only a few yards away from him, stood the Witch
paragraphs.mainIdea: Digory finds the Witch in the garden. She has eaten an apple, and she looks stronger and prouder, but her face is deadly white.
paragraphs.simple: Digory was just turning to go back to the gates when he stopped to have one last look round. He got a terrible shock. He was not alone. Only a few yards away from him stood the Witch. She was just throwing away the core of an apple that she had eaten. The juice was darker than you would expect and had made a horrible stain round her mouth. Digory guessed at once that she must have climbed in over the wall. He began to see that there might be some sense in that last line about getting your heart's desire and getting despair along with it. The Witch looked stronger and prouder than ever, and even, in a way, like a winner. But her face was deadly white, as white as salt.

paragraphs.context: one bite of that apple would heal her
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Witch tells Digory to take the apple to his Mother. She says it would make her well and that his home would be happy again.
paragraphs.simple: The Witch said, "Do you not see, Fool, that one bite of that apple would make her well? You have it in your pocket. We are here by ourselves, and the Lion is far away. Use your Magic and go back to your own world. A minute later you can be at your Mother's bedside, giving her the fruit. Five minutes later you will see the color coming back to her face. She will tell you the pain is gone. Soon she will tell you she feels stronger. Then she will fall asleep. Think of that: hours of sweet, natural sleep, without pain, without drugs. Next day everyone will be saying how well she has got. Soon she will be quite well again. All will be well again. Your home will be happy again. You will be like other boys."

paragraphs.context: let it be your first care to guard this Tree
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan tells the Narnians to guard the Tree. While it grows well, the Witch will not come near it, because its smell is death and horror to her.
paragraphs.simple: Aslan said, "Son of Adam, you have sown well. And you, Narnians, make it your first care to guard this Tree, for it is your Shield. The Witch of whom I told you has run far away into the North of the world. She will live on there, growing stronger in dark Magic. But while that tree grows well, she will never come down into Narnia. She dare not come within a hundred miles of the Tree, for its smell, which is joy and life and health to you, is death and horror and despair to her."

paragraphs.context: Things always work according to their nature
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan says that the fruit does work for the Witch: she has strength and endless days. But a long life with an evil heart is only a long misery.
paragraphs.simple: "Alas," said Aslan, and he shook his head. "It will. Things always work according to their nature. She has won her heart's desire. She has strength that never tires and endless days, like a goddess. But a long life with an evil heart is only a long misery, and already she begins to know it. All get what they want; they do not always like it."

paragraphs.context: great nations in your world will be ruled by tyrants
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan says that the children's world is growing more like Charn. He warns that tyrants will rule great nations, and he tells the children to bury the magic rings.
paragraphs.simple: Aslan said, "Not yet, Daughter of Eve. But you are growing more like it. It is not certain that some wicked one of your race will not find out a secret as evil as the Deplorable Word and use it to destroy all living things. And very soon, before you are an old man and an old woman, great nations in your world will be ruled by tyrants. They will care no more for joy and justice and mercy than the Empress Jadis. Let your world beware. That is the warning. Now for the command. As soon as you can, take from your Uncle his magic rings and bury them, so that no one can use them again."

paragraphs.context: a real, natural, gentle sleep, without any of those nasty drugs
paragraphs.mainIdea: Digory's Mother eats the apple and falls into a real, natural sleep. Digory thinks her face looks different, and he begins to hope.
paragraphs.simple: Digory peeled the apple, cut it up and gave it to his Mother piece by piece. As soon as she had finished it, she smiled, her head went back on the pillow, and she was asleep. It was a real, natural, gentle sleep, without any of those nasty drugs. Digory knew that this was the thing she wanted most in the whole world. He was sure now that her face looked a little different. He bent down and kissed her very softly and went quietly out of the room with a beating heart, taking the core of the apple with him. For the rest of that day, when he looked at the things around him and saw how ordinary they were, with no magic in them, he hardly dared to hope. But when he remembered the face of Aslan, he did hope.

paragraphs.context: That was the beginning of all the comings and goings between Narnia and our world
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree that grew from the apple core in England had apples that were not fully magical. A storm blew it down, and Digory had a wardrobe made from its wood. That began the comings and goings between Narnia and our world.
paragraphs.simple: The tree that grew from the core of the Apple that Digory planted in the back garden grew into a fine tree. It grew in the soil of our world, far from the sound of Aslan's voice and far from the young air of Narnia. So it did not bear apples that could bring a dying woman back to health, as Digory's Mother had been. It did bear apples more beautiful than any others in England, and they were extremely good for you, though not fully magical. But inside itself, in its sap, the tree never forgot that other tree in Narnia. Sometimes it would move when there was no wind. The writer thinks this happened when there were high winds in Narnia, and the English tree shook because the Narnia tree was rocking in a strong southwestern gale. Later it was proved that there was still magic in its wood. When Digory was quite middle-aged, a famous learned man, a Professor and a great traveler, the old house of the Ketterleys belonged to him. Then a great storm all over the south of England blew the tree down. He could not bear to have it simply chopped up for firewood, so he had part of the wood made into a wardrobe, which he put in his big house in the country. He did not find the magic of that wardrobe himself, but someone else did. That was the beginning of all the comings and goings between Narnia and our world, which you can read about in other books.

sentences.context: It could hardly have been grubbier if he had first rubbed his hands in the earth
sentences.simple: His face could hardly have been dirtier if he had first rubbed his hands in the earth, then had a good cry, and then dried his face with his hands.
sentences.grammar: 'Could hardly have been dirtier' means it was almost as dirty as possible; 'if he had first rubbed ...' imagines what he might have done.

sentences.context: If vacuum cleaners had been invented in those days Polly would have thought
sentences.simple: Vacuum cleaners were not invented then. If they had been, Polly would have thought the sound was a Hoover working a long way off, several rooms away and several floors below.
sentences.grammar: 'If + had been invented, would have thought' talks about something that did not happen: they were not invented, so Polly did not think that.

sentences.context: for the door had been made for getting in, not for getting out
sentences.simple: There was no bolt or handle on this side of the door, because it had been made for getting in, not for getting out.
sentences.grammar: 'Had been made' is 'had been + past form' (it was made before that time); 'for + -ing' says what the door was for.

sentences.context: Polly was very surprised because up till now there had never been any children in that house
sentences.simple: Polly was very surprised, because until now there had never been any children in that house. Only Mr. Ketterley and Miss Ketterley lived there.
sentences.grammar: 'Had never been' ('had + past form') means that up to that moment in the past it was never so; 'up till now' means 'until now'.

sentences.context: that had ever happened to Digory even in a nightmare, that he let out a scream
sentences.simple: It was so sudden, and so horribly unlike anything that had ever happened to Digory, even in a nightmare, that he screamed.
sentences.grammar: 'So ... that' shows a result: it was so sudden and strange that he screamed; 'had ever happened' looks back over all his past.

sentences.context: if someone else will go after her, wearing a yellow ring himself
sentences.simple: She can get back if someone else is willing to go after her. He must wear a yellow ring himself and take two green rings, one to bring himself back and one to bring her back.
sentences.grammar: 'If someone else will go' uses 'will' in the if-part to mean 'is willing to go'; 'wearing' and 'taking' tell how he must go.

sentences.context: A man at my time of life, and in my state of health, to risk the shock
sentences.simple: Uncle Andrew asks: Should a man of my age and my state of health risk the shock and the dangers of being thrown suddenly into a different universe?
sentences.grammar: This is a question with no 'should'. It means 'Should a man of my age ... risk ...?'

sentences.context: he was neither dripping nor panting for breath as anyone would expect
sentences.simple: He was not dripping with water and he was not out of breath, as anyone would expect after being under water.
sentences.grammar: 'Neither ... nor' means not this and not that; 'as anyone would expect' says it is what people normally think.

sentences.context: if we can get back to our own world by jumping into this pool, mightn’t we get somewhere else
sentences.simple: If we can get back to our own world by jumping into this pool, maybe we can get somewhere else by jumping into one of the other pools.
sentences.grammar: 'Mightn't we ...?' is a question that means 'maybe we can'; 'by + -ing' tells how (by jumping).

sentences.context: a place that isn’t in any of the worlds, but once you’ve found that place
sentences.simple: This wood might be the same: a place that is not in any of the worlds. But once you have found that place, you can get into all of them.
sentences.grammar: 'Once you’ve found' (once + present perfect) means 'after you have found'; 'but' shows a different idea from the first part.

sentences.context: the chances would have been a hundred to one against their ever finding it again
sentences.simple: If they had left the pool that led to our own world without making some sort of landmark, it would have been a hundred to one against their ever finding it again.
sentences.grammar: 'If they had left ..., it would have been ...' talks about something that did not happen; 'a hundred to one against' means very unlikely.

sentences.context: If only Digory had remembered what he himself had said a few minutes ago
sentences.simple: Digory had said a few minutes earlier that this was an enchanted room. If he had remembered that, he might have guessed that the enchantment was beginning to work.
sentences.grammar: 'If only + had + past form' shows a wish about the past: he did not remember it; 'might have guessed' means it was possible.

sentences.context: We shall always be wondering what else would have happened if we had struck the bell
sentences.simple: We will always be wondering what else would have happened if we had struck the bell.
sentences.grammar: 'Shall always be wondering' means it goes on and on in the future; 'would have happened if we had struck' talks about something that did not happen.

sentences.context: If we are not out of it in a few minutes we shall be buried under the ruin
sentences.simple: If we are not out of the palace in a few minutes, we will be buried under the ruin.
sentences.grammar: 'If + present, shall be + past form' is a real future condition; 'shall be buried' means the ruin will fall on us and bury us.

sentences.context: there was a word which, if spoken with the proper ceremonies, would destroy all living things
sentences.simple: There was a word that would destroy all living things, except the one who spoke it, if it was spoken with the proper ceremonies.
sentences.grammar: 'If spoken' is short for 'if it was spoken'; 'which ... would destroy' tells what the word could do.

sentences.context: though it were a thousand years, till one came and struck the bell and awoke me
sentences.simple: Jadis had put strong spells on the hall. They made her sleep among the images like an image herself, with no need of food or fire, even for a thousand years, until someone came and struck the bell and woke her.
sentences.grammar: 'Though it were' is an old way to say 'even if it was' (an imagined case); 'neither ... nor' means not this and not that; 'till' means 'until'.

sentences.context: any more than you’d be afraid of a worm after you had met a rattlesnake
sentences.simple: After seeing the two together, you would never again be afraid of Uncle Andrew. You would be no more afraid of him than of a worm after meeting a rattlesnake, or of a cow after meeting a mad bull.
sentences.grammar: 'No more ... than' puts two things side by side: you are not afraid of the first, just as you are not afraid of the second; 'after you had met' shows the meeting comes first.

sentences.context: I will lay such spells on you that anything you sit down on will feel like red hot iron
sentences.simple: At the first sign that you do not obey, I will put such spells on you that anything you sit on will feel like red hot iron. Whenever you lie in a bed, there will be invisible blocks of ice at your feet.
sentences.grammar: 'Such ... that' shows a result: the spells will be so strong that these things happen; 'whenever' means every time.

sentences.context: It must have been a terrible moment for the Witch when she suddenly realized
sentences.simple: It must have been a terrible moment for the Witch. She suddenly saw that her power of turning people into dust, which had been quite real in her own world, was not going to work in ours.
sentences.grammar: 'Must have + past form' is a strong guess about the past; 'was not going to work' says what she found would not happen.

sentences.context: she must not be allowed to go rampaging about the house
sentences.simple: No matter what happened, she must not be allowed to go rushing wildly about the house.
sentences.grammar: 'Must not be allowed to' means 'we must not let her'; 'Whatever happened' means 'no matter what'.

sentences.context: If he had heard that bit about the land of youth a few days ago he would have thought
sentences.simple: If Digory had heard about the land of youth a few days earlier, he would have thought Aunt Letty was just talking without meaning anything, as grown-ups do. It would not have interested him.
sentences.grammar: 'If + had heard, would have thought' talks about something that did not happen: he did not hear it then, so this is what would have happened.

sentences.context: if we’ve fallen down some diggings—as it might be for a new station on the Underground
sentences.simple: If we have fallen down some diggings, as it might be for a new station on the Underground, someone will come and get us out soon.
sentences.grammar: 'As it might be' gives an example (like 'for instance'); 'if we’ve fallen' is a real possibility, so the result uses 'will'.

sentences.context: he gave the sort of whinny a horse would give if, after years of being a cab-horse
sentences.simple: The horse made the kind of sound a horse would make if, after years of being a cab-horse, it found itself back in the old field where it had played as a young horse, and saw someone it remembered and loved coming across the field to bring it a lump of sugar.
sentences.grammar: 'Would give if ... found' is an imagined case; 'after years of being' is 'after + -ing'; 'had played' is earlier than 'found'.

sentences.context: She would have had her hands in Digory’s pocket before you could say knife
sentences.simple: She would have had her hands in Digory’s pocket before you could say knife, but Digory grabbed Polly and shouted out.
sentences.grammar: 'Would have had' shows what nearly happened but did not; 'before you could say knife' is an idiom for 'very quickly'.

sentences.context: You have not made the first joke; you have only been the first joke
sentences.simple: You have not made the first joke. You have only been the first joke.
sentences.grammar: 'Make a joke' (say something funny) is different from 'be a joke' (be the thing people laugh at); 'have not made / have been' is the present perfect.

sentences.context: you need not always be grave
sentences.simple: Now that you can speak and think, you do not always have to be serious.
sentences.grammar: 'Need not' means 'do not have to'; 'Now that' gives the reason.

sentences.context: And as Adam’s race has done the harm, Adam’s race shall help to heal it
sentences.simple: Adam’s race has done the harm, so Adam’s race will help to heal it.
sentences.grammar: 'As' here means 'because'; 'shall' is a strong promise or order that something will happen.

sentences.context: Are you ready to undo the wrong that you have done to my sweet country
sentences.simple: Are you ready to put right the wrong that you have done to my dear country of Narnia on the very day it began?
sentences.grammar: 'Ready to + verb' asks if he is willing to act; 'that you have done' (present perfect) tells which wrong, one that still matters now.

sentences.context: It would have been better if he had not
sentences.simple: It would have been better if Digory had not looked at the apple and smelled it.
sentences.grammar: 'Would have been better if he had not' talks about the past: he did it, and it was a mistake.

sentences.context: She was just throwing away the core of an apple which she had eaten
sentences.simple: She was just throwing away the core of an apple that she had eaten.
sentences.grammar: 'Was throwing' ('was + verb-ing') is the action in progress; 'had eaten' ('had + past form') happened before it.

sentences.context: that is why all the rest are now a horror to her
sentences.simple: That is the reason all the other apples are now a horror to her.
sentences.grammar: 'That is why' gives the reason for what was just said; 'all the rest' means all the other ones.

sentences.context: All get what they want; they do not always like it
sentences.simple: All people get what they want, but they do not always like it.
sentences.grammar: 'What they want' means 'the things that they want' and comes after 'get'; the semicolon joins two opposite ideas.

sentences.context: if ever they were sad or afraid or angry, the thought of all that golden goodness
sentences.simple: As long as they both lived, if they were ever sad or afraid or angry, the thought of all that golden goodness would come back and make them sure that all was well.
sentences.grammar: 'If ever' means 'whenever'; 'would come back' shows something that happened again and again; 'as long as' means 'for all the time that'.

sentences.context: there was a great storm all over the south of England which blew the tree down
sentences.simple: A great storm came all over the south of England, and it blew the tree down.
sentences.grammar: 'Which blew the tree down' tells more about the storm; 'blew down' is a verb + small word that means 'made fall by wind'.

shut up.meaning: To stop talking (an unkind way to say it). It can also mean to keep a person inside a place.

look after.example: they were looking after your Mother

break down.example: My health broke down in the end.

find out.meaning: To learn a fact that you did not know.

let go.example: she let go of his chin

go on.example: How long does this tunnel go on for?

hold on.example: Hold on to me tight, Polly.

take notice of.meaning: To pay attention to a person or thing.

make it up.meaning: To be friends again after a fight.

get hold of.example: to get hold of her yellow ring

get to know.meaning: To begin to know a person.

see through.meaning: To know the truth about a person who is not honest.
see through.example: he saw through Uncle Andrew’s grand words

in vain.example: struggled in vain with the hat

give in.meaning: To stop fighting against something and let it win.
give in.example: If we once give in to it

put on.meaning: To place clothes or a ring on your body to wear.
put on.example: They put on their green rings

pick up.meaning: To take something up with your hand.

take off.meaning: To remove something you are wearing.
take off.example: Let’s take off our green rings

slip on.meaning: To put something on quickly and easily.

make a fuss.meaning: To show strongly that you do not like something.
make a fuss.example: made rather a fuss about agreeing

by the way.meaning: Used to add something new to what you are saying.
by the way.example: By the way, how do we get home?

as a matter of fact.example: this was very nearly what he had been doing

give up.meaning: To stop having something such as hope.

talk over.example: when they had talked it over

in charge of.meaning: Having the job of looking after a person or thing.
in charge of.example: Are you in charge of that there young woman?

come on.meaning: Used to tell someone to go fast or to come with you.

look out.meaning: To be careful; or to watch for something.

get rid of.meaning: To free yourself of a person or thing.
get rid of.example: we’ve got rid of that woman

take a deep breath.meaning: To take in a lot of air.
take a deep breath.example: took a deep breath, and picked up the ring

drive mad.meaning: To make a person feel crazy.
drive mad.example: Or wonder, till it drives you mad

stand still.meaning: To stay in one place and not move.

what on earth.meaning: Used in a question to show that you are very surprised.
what on earth.example: what on earth had happened to them both
